q: A doctor plots patient cases on a map to check whether a suspected water source explains an outbreak. Which visualization goal is this?
a: Confirm a hypothesis
e: You already have a guess (the water source) and use the picture to test it, like John Snow's cholera map.

q: A journalist designs a chart so readers instantly grasp how many soldiers died of disease versus wounds. Which goal is this?
a: Communicate ideas to others
e: The insight is already known; the chart's job is to get it across to an audience (like Nightingale's diagrams).

q: An analyst explores a migration dataset with no specific question, looking for patterns worth investigating. Which goal fits best?
a: Analyze data to support reasoning
e: Open-ended exploration to support reasoning, rather than testing a specific guess or presenting a finished message.

q: Sketching a specimen or photographing motion frames (like Muybridge's horse) mainly serves which goal?
a: Record information
e: Recording captures information so it can be kept and studied later.

q: Why is finding the most frequent number faster in a bar chart than in a grid of numbers?
a: Perception does the work in parallel instead of reading and counting values one by one
w: Bar charts contain more data than tables
Numbers are harder to print than bars
e: Visualization offloads work from limited cognition and working memory onto fast visual perception.

q: Visualization 'enhances working memory' mainly because:
a: The picture acts as external memory you can look back at instead of holding values in your head
w: It permanently increases how much you can remember
It removes the need to look at the data
It compresses the data into fewer values
e: Like doing multiplication on paper, the display stores intermediate information for you.

q: The lecture warns that perception can point out interesting things 'but can also deceive you.' What's the practical lesson?
a: Design choices can create patterns that aren't in the data, so encodings must be chosen carefully
w: Visualization should be avoided for important decisions
Only statistics can be trusted, never charts
Perception is too slow for large datasets
e: The same power that makes patterns pop out can make false patterns pop out.

q: Anscombe argued computers should produce both calculations and graphs. What's the main reason?
a: Datasets with identical summary statistics can look completely different when plotted
w: Graphs are always more accurate than statistics
Calculations are too slow without graphs
Graphs replace the need for statistics
e: Summary statistics can hide structure (outliers, curves, clusters) that a plot reveals.

q: Because only the fovea sees sharply and the eye jumps between fixations, what design advice follows?
a: Avoid cramming too much data on screen; crisp, clear visuals are interpreted best
w: Use as much detail as possible since the eye scans everything
Put key information at the edges of the screen
Use blur to guide attention away from the center
e: We only see a small area in detail at a time, and the brain fills in the rest.

q: Your brain 'fills in' the blind spot and peripheral blur. What does this imply for reading a visualization?
a: Viewers may believe they saw details they never actually looked at
w: Peripheral vision is best for reading labels
The blind spot only matters in 3D charts
e: Vision is limited at any moment; the brain reconstructs the rest.

q: Mach bands and the Cornsweet illusion show that the visual system mainly responds to:
a: Edges and differences, not absolute brightness
w: The average color of a region
e: Receptive fields enhance edges, so perceived brightness depends on contrast at boundaries.

q: If the outlines of shapes are important in your chart, the lecture advises you to:
a: Maximize contrast with the background
w: Match the shape color to the background
e: Since we're tuned to edges, strong contrast makes boundaries clear.

q: Weber's law says we judge relative differences. Which comparison is EASIEST?
a: Two bars sitting on a common baseline next to each other
w: Two bars on different baselines far apart
Two unaligned bars of nearly equal length
Two circles of slightly different area
e: Aligning items on a common axis turns the judgment into a small, relative difference that's easy to see.

q: Two identical gray squares look different because one sits on a dark background and one on a light one. This is:
a: Simultaneous contrast
e: Judgments of brightness and color are relative to the local surroundings.

q: Given simultaneous contrast, what should you do when encoding values with gray levels or color?
a: Avoid placing marks on varying or busy backgrounds; keep the context neutral
w: Use a rainbow background to boost contrast
Put each mark on a different colored background
Rely on viewers judging absolute brightness
e: Do your best not to place data in difficult contexts; choose position and background carefully.

q: You want one important point to stand out among hundreds. Which approach works best?
a: Make it differ in a single strong channel, like a unique color
w: Make it differ in both color and shape from different distractors
Make it slightly larger than the rest
Hide it among similar shapes with a label
e: Popout works on one strong feature contrast; conjunctions of features need slow serial search.

q: A target is the only red circle among red squares and blue circles. Why is it slow to find?
a: It's a conjunction of features, which requires serial search instead of popping out
w: Red is a weak pre-attentive channel
e: Each distractor shares one feature with the target, so no single channel separates it.

q: What matters most for something to pop out pre-attentively?
a: Strong contrast between the target's feature and the surrounding features
w: The total number of colors used
The size of the whole chart
Whether the viewer reads the legend
e: Pop-out depends on feature contrast, not on how much is on screen.

q: Why should color and shape be used sparingly for highlighting?
a: If many things are highlighted, nothing stands out
w: Browsers limit the number of colors
e: Popout depends on contrast with everything else; overusing it destroys that contrast.

q: In a scatterplot, you draw a box around a cluster of points to show they belong together. Which Gestalt principle are you using?
a: Enclosure
e: Elements inside a common boundary are perceived as a group.

q: A line chart connects each country's yearly points with a line, so we read them as one series. Which principle?
a: Connection
e: Visually connected elements are perceived as related, and connection is a very strong grouping cue.

q: Using the same color for all bars belonging to one category relies on:
a: Similarity
e: Things that look alike (color, size, shape) are perceived as related.

q: Leaving extra space between groups of bars in a grouped bar chart uses which principle?
a: Proximity
e: Items close together are seen as a group; gaps separate groups.

q: In an animated chart, points that move together are seen as a cluster. Which principle?
a: Common fate
e: Elements moving in the same direction are perceived as a unit.

q: A line passes behind a label, but viewers still see one continuous line. Which principle?
a: Continuity
e: We complete hidden objects into simple, familiar shapes.

q: A busy background makes it unclear which marks are data and which are decoration. Which principle is being violated?
a: Figure/ground
e: Elements are perceived as either figure or background; data should clearly be the figure.

q: What's the risk of using Gestalt principles carelessly?
a: Viewers may see groupings or relationships that aren't in the data
e: Poor use may cause users to see things that aren't there.

q: You're tuning a chart color by hand and want to make it 'less vivid' without changing what color it is. Which model makes that easiest?
a: HSV/HSL (reduce saturation)
e: HSV is more intuitive for tuning: hue = which color, saturation = how much white, value/lightness = how much black.

q: Why is RGB a poor space for building a colormap where equal steps should look equally different?
a: It isn't perceptually uniform, and the actual color depends on the device
e: Equal numeric steps in RGB don't produce equal perceived steps.

q: Which color space is designed so distances roughly match perceived differences?
a: CIE LAB
e: LAB is mathematically defined and perceptually based: L* lightness, a red–green, b yellow–blue.

q: Printing a chart on paper uses which kind of color mixing?
a: Subtractive (CMY + K)
e: Ink absorbs light, so print is subtractive; K gives a true black.

q: In HSV terms, a pastel color is one with:
a: Low saturation (more white mixed in)
e: Saturation is the amount of white mixed in; pastels have little saturation.

q: A chart uses red for 'loss' and green for 'gain' and nothing else. What's the main accessibility problem?
a: The most common color deficiencies make red and green hard to tell apart
w: Green has low luminance contrast with white
e: Deuteranomaly (most common) and protanomaly both impair red–green discrimination.

q: Which fix best makes a red/green chart readable for colorblind viewers?
a: Also vary luminance or add a second cue like shape or labels
w: Make the red and green more saturated
e: Design with colorblindness in mind: vary hue, saturation and brightness, or use cues besides color.

q: Maureen Stone's advice 'get it right in black and white' means:
a: The chart should still work if color is removed, so luminance carries the key structure
w: Black and white printers are the target audience
e: If it works without hue, luminance differences are doing the heavy lifting, which also helps colorblind viewers.

q: You need fine detail (thin lines, small text) to be readable. Which channel should carry it?
a: Luminance (light vs. dark contrast)
e: We have higher contrast sensitivity for luminance than for chrominance.

q: Gray text on a slightly lighter gray background is hard to read. What does the lecture's guideline say?
a: Aim for about 10:1 luminance contrast, never below 3:1
w: Any contrast is fine if the hue differs
e: Text needs strong luminance contrast to be legible.

q: Small scatterplot points in pale colors are hard to tell apart. Why?
a: The smaller the mark, the harder colors are to distinguish
e: Bertin: color differences shrink with mark size. Use brighter, more saturated colors for small marks.

q: Which saturation choice fits each use: large background areas vs. small points?
a: Low-saturation pastels for large areas; bright, saturated colors for small marks
w: Saturated colors for large areas; pastels for small marks
e: Large saturated areas are overwhelming; small marks need saturation to be visible.

q: You're coloring countries by political party (5 parties). What kind of colormap fits?
a: Categorical hues, one distinct hue per party
w: A diverging map centered on zero
A rainbow ramp ordered by party size
e: Hue has no inherent order, which suits categorical data. Keep it to about 6–12 hues.

q: You're coloring counties by median income. Which colormap fits?
a: Sequential: vary luminance and/or saturation from low to high
w: A rainbow from red to violet
e: Ordered data needs a channel with an inherent order, like luminance or saturation.

q: You're showing temperature change relative to a baseline, with warmer and cooler values. Which colormap fits?
a: Diverging: two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint for zero change
e: A diverging map makes the meaningful midpoint (zero change) explicit.

q: Why are rainbow colormaps discouraged for continuous data?
a: Perceived contrast is uneven and they have no explicit midpoint or natural order
e: Rainbow creates false boundaries and hides others; people don't agree on its order.

q: A design uses 20 different hues to label 20 categories. What's the problem?
a: People can only reliably tell apart about 6–12 colors at once
e: Beyond about 6–12 hues, categories become confusable; consider grouping or other channels.

q: Why are nameable colors (red, blue, orange) better for categories than subtle shades?
a: They're easier to remember and refer to
e: Categorical colors are easier to remember if they're nameable.

q: A bivariate colormap mixes two continuous variables into one color. When does this work reasonably?
a: When at least one of the variables is binary
w: When using a rainbow for each
e: Bivariate colormaps are hard to read unless one variable has only two values.

q: 'Expressiveness' for colormaps means:
a: Match the colormap type to the attribute type (categorical, sequential, diverging)
w: Use as many colors as possible
e: The colormap should express exactly the structure the data has, no more and no less.

q: A dashboard uses five bright colors equally for everything. What does the 'simplicity' guideline suggest?
a: Pick one base color used in larger amounts and use others sparingly for interest
e: Be selective about the base color and use accents sparingly.

q: When color isn't needed, what does the lecture suggest instead?
a: Use neutrals and other channels like size, shape or position
w: Use a rainbow to be safe
e: Avoidance of color: neutrals work with any scheme, and diagrammatic marks may be better channels.

q: Ordinal data is encoded with color. Where should the marks be placed?
a: On a solid, neutral background
e: Color is relative; a neutral background avoids contrast effects shifting perceived values.

q: Why describe data in abstract terms (items, attributes) instead of domain terms (patients, genes)?
a: It lets you reuse design knowledge across domains and reason systematically about the design space
w: It hides the meaning from users
e: Abstract vocabulary avoids domain-specific terms, so the what-why-how framework applies anywhere.

q: In the what-why-how framework, choosing between a bar chart and a heatmap is part of:
a: How (the encoding and interaction)
e: What = data, why = the user's task, how = the visual encoding and interaction.

q: A spreadsheet of students with columns for name, age and major. What are the rows and columns?
a: Rows are items; columns are attributes
w: Rows are attributes; columns are items
Rows are links; columns are positions
Rows are grids; columns are fields
e: In a table, each row is an item and each column is an attribute.

q: A social network of friendships between people is which dataset type?
a: Network: items (nodes) connected by links
e: Networks consist of items (nodes) and links, both of which can have attributes.

q: Wind measurements (speed and direction) at every point of a weather grid are best described as:
a: A field with vector attributes
e: Fields have values at cells across continuous space; direction plus magnitude is a vector.

q: Temperature measured at every cell of a 3D grid is a field with what kind of attribute?
a: Scalar
e: A single number per cell is scalar; direction+magnitude is a vector; a matrix per cell is a tensor.

q: When visualizing a continuous field from sampled points, which two choices shape what viewers see?
a: Sampling (where values are measured) and interpolation (how values in between are modeled)
e: Grid choices affect how continuous data is interpreted.

q: Blood type (A, B, AB, O) is which attribute type?
a: Categorical
e: There's no inherent order among blood types.

q: Survey answers 'disagree, neutral, agree' are which attribute type?
a: Ordinal
e: They have a clear order, but the 'distance' between levels isn't a meaningful number.

q: Height in centimeters is which attribute type?
a: Quantitative
e: It has a meaningful magnitude, so arithmetic (differences, averages) makes sense.

q: Which test tells ordinal and quantitative apart?
a: Whether arithmetic like differences and averages is meaningful
w: Whether there are more than 5 values
e: Both can be ordered; only quantitative data has meaningful magnitudes.

q: Month of the year (Jan … Dec, then back to Jan) is an ordered attribute that is:
a: Cyclic
e: It wraps around, so the end connects back to the start.

q: Profit, where values range from losses through zero to gains, is an ordered attribute that is:
a: Diverging
e: There's a meaningful midpoint (zero) with values going in two directions.

q: You convert exact temperatures into 'hot, warm, cold'. What have you created, and why might you?
a: A derived ordinal attribute that simplifies the data for the task
w: A categorical attribute with no order
e: Derived attributes are computed from the originals; the transformation is an abstraction choice.

q: Turning temperature into 'above freezing / below freezing' produces which attribute type?
a: Categorical (binary)
e: Two groups with no meaningful magnitude between them.

q: What's the difference between the data model and the conceptual model?
a: The data model is the math type (e.g., floats); the conceptual model is what the values mean (e.g., temperature)
w: The data model is the chart; the conceptual model is the file
The conceptual model is the database schema
e: Knowing the meaning (conceptual model) motivates which abstraction to choose.

q: In a scatterplot, what are the marks and what are the channels?
a: Points are the marks; horizontal and vertical position are the channels
w: Axes are the marks; points are the channels
Colors are the marks; lines are the channels
Labels are the marks; the grid is the channel
e: Marks are graphical elements; channels control their appearance.

q: In a bar chart, what are the marks and which channel encodes the value?
a: Lines (bars) as marks; length/vertical position encodes the value
w: Points as marks; color encodes the value
Areas as marks; shape encodes the value
Text as marks; angle encodes the value
e: Each bar is a mark whose length shows the quantity.

q: A choropleth map uses which mark type for regions?
a: Areas (2D)
e: Marks are classified by spatial dimension: points 0D, lines 1D, areas 2D.

q: You need to show product categories (no order). Which channel type fits?
a: An identity channel like hue, shape or spatial region
e: Expressiveness: identity channels for categorical data, magnitude channels for ordered data.

q: Why is encoding a quantitative value with shape a bad idea?
a: Shape has no inherent order or magnitude, so it can't express 'how much'
w: Shape is the most accurate channel
e: Shape is an identity channel; it can't convey magnitude.

q: You want viewers to compare values as accurately as possible. Which channel should you use?
a: Position on a common scale
e: Position on a common scale is the most effective magnitude channel.

q: Why is a bar chart usually more accurate than a pie chart for comparing values?
a: Length/position is judged more accurately than angle or area
e: In the effectiveness ranking, position and length outrank angle and area.

q: Which magnitude channel ranks lowest in effectiveness?
a: Volume (3D size)
e: Curvature and volume are at the bottom of the ranking.

q: Effectiveness says the most important attribute should get:
a: The most effective channel (e.g., position)
w: The least effective channel, to save space
e: Rank attributes by importance and assign the best channels to the most important ones.

q: Channel effectiveness rankings mostly come from:
a: Perception experiments measuring how accurately people judge each channel
e: Rankings come from studies like Cleveland & McGill and crowdsourced experiments.

q: You encode 15 levels of a variable using line width. What's the concern?
a: Discriminability: viewers can't reliably tell that many widths apart
w: Line width is an identity channel
e: Each channel supports only a limited number of distinguishable steps.

q: You map one variable to a rectangle's width and another to its height. What happens?
a: They're integral, so viewers see overall area/shape instead of each variable separately
w: Each is read independently with no interference
e: Width and height are integral channels, perceived holistically.

q: Which pair of channels is separable, so each can be read independently?
a: Color and position
e: Separable channels can be judged individually; integral ones fuse.

q: A 3D bar chart makes back bars look smaller and hides some behind others. Which problems are these?
a: Perspective distortion of size and occlusion
w: Low data-ink ratio and chart junk
e: 3D adds perspective cues that interfere with size and color, plus occlusion and poor text legibility.

q: When is animation a GOOD choice?
a: Storytelling and smooth transitions between views
w: Comparing many states with many changes
e: Animation is good for narrative and transitions, bad for detailed comparison.

q: You want readers to compare how 12 regions changed across 10 years. Which is better?
a: Small multiples, so they can compare by moving their eyes
w: An animation that plays each year
A pie chart per year shown one at a time
e: Comparing views side by side uses the display as external memory; animation forces comparison against memory.

q: A chart shows a 20% increase in the data, but the bar grows to look 100% bigger. What's the Lie Factor?
e: Lie Factor = size of effect shown in the graphic ÷ size of effect in the data. Ideally it's 1.

q: Icons are scaled by height (diameter) to show values twice as large. What goes wrong?
a: Area grows four times, so the difference looks exaggerated
w: The difference looks smaller than it is
e: Area scales with the square of the linear size, so scale by area, not by diameter.

q: A bar chart's y-axis starts at 95 instead of 0, making a small change look dramatic. When is a non-zero baseline acceptable?
a: When zero isn't meaningful, to show relative position, or where it's the norm (like stock charts)
e: Bars encode length from a baseline, so truncation distorts them unless zero doesn't make sense.

q: A chart shows numbers without any axis or baseline. Why is that a problem?
a: Without a scale or baseline, viewers can't judge the true size of differences
e: Missing scales hide distortion; clear labeling defeats ambiguity.

q: 'Show data variation, not design variation' warns against:
a: Changing visual design (like icon size or style) in ways that look like changes in data
e: Unintended size coding makes design differences read as data differences.

q: A chart shows a stock dropping sharply, but the full history shows it's a small dip. What's missing?
a: Context (a longer time range or comparison)
e: Insufficient context can make normal variation look like a crash.

q: One value is 100× bigger than the rest and squashes everything else flat. Which is a reasonable fix?
a: Use a log scale or a scale break (or clip it and say so)
e: Clipping, scale breaks and log scales are the lecture's options. Always be transparent.

q: Why use a log scale when data spans several orders of magnitude?
a: Equal distances show equal ratios, so small and large values are both readable
w: It makes all values look equal
e: Log scales show multiplicative change and keep small values from being flattened.

q: Removing heavy gridlines, borders and shading while keeping the data is an example of:
a: Maximizing the data-ink ratio
e: Data-ink ratio = ink used for data ÷ total ink. Erase non-data ink when it adds nothing.

q: A study found the most minimal box plot (highest data-ink ratio) was hardest to interpret. What's the lesson?
a: Maximizing data-ink isn't always best; some 'redundant' ink helps comprehension
w: Box plots should never be used
Data-ink ratio is unrelated to design
e: The counterpoint shows data-ink is a guideline, not a law.

q: Research on embellished 'chart junk' found it can help with:
a: Long-term memorability and engagement
e: Embellished charts were recalled better weeks later; the cons are interpretability, trust and space.

q: When is chart junk most defensible?
a: When the goal is persuasion, memorability or engagement rather than careful analysis
e: Chart junk? It depends: pros are persuasion, memorability and engagement.

q: Data density = data entries ÷ area of the graphic. How does Tufte suggest increasing it?
a: Shrink the graphics, e.g., with small multiples or sparklines
w: Spread the data over more pages
e: Show more data in the same space.

q: A trellis plot splits data into a grid of small charts. Which variables usually define the grid?
a: Categorical or ordinal variables
e: Subdivide by nominal/ordinal variables so each panel compares like with like.

q: A designer adds many extra visual features, assuming viewers will take it all in at once. Which illusion is this?
a: Overestimate of breadth
e: Viewers can't absorb everything at once, and extra features make specific information harder to find.

q: A designer assumes users will look at every part of a dashboard, but they only look where they expect. Which illusion?
a: Overestimate of countenance
e: Users attend to less of the display than designers think.

q: A designer assumes that because users looked at a chart, they understood it fully. Which illusion?
a: Overestimate of depth
e: Attending to something doesn't mean deep understanding.

q: A 3D pie chart makes a smaller slice in front look bigger than a larger slice behind it. Why?
a: Perspective distorts slice areas, so front slices look larger
e: 3D perspective changes apparent size; a flat bar chart avoids it.

q: Why are dual-axis charts risky?
a: Each axis can be scaled independently, so lines can be made to cross or diverge to suggest false relationships
e: The crossing point is an artifact of the chosen scales, not of the data.

q: Tufte's graphical excellence aims to give viewers:
a: The most ideas, in the shortest time, with the least ink, in the smallest space
w: The most colors in the largest space
e: It's about efficient communication: as simple as possible, but no simpler.

q: 'Find which states have unusually high unemployment' as an {action, target} pair is:
a: {locate/identify, outliers}
e: Tasks are abstracted as an action plus a target.

q: A news graphic that tells readers a finished story serves which consume goal?
a: Present
e: Present = communicate something already known; discover = find new insight; enjoy = casual interest.

q: A researcher uses a tool to find new patterns nobody knew about. Which consume goal?
a: Discover
e: Discover means generating or verifying new hypotheses.

q: A beautiful live wind map people browse just for fun serves which goal?
a: Enjoy
e: Casual, curiosity-driven use with no specific task.

q: You know the name of the city you're looking for but not where it is on the map. Which search task?
a: Locate
e: Target known, location unknown = locate.

q: You know both what you're looking for and where it is (e.g., a specific cell in a table). Which search task?
a: Lookup
e: Target known, location known = lookup.

q: You scan a particular region of a chart without a specific target in mind. Which search task?
a: Browse
e: Location known, target unknown = browse.

q: You have no specific target and don't know where to look. Which search task?
a: Explore
e: Neither target nor location known = explore.

q: You look at one data point, then two, then the whole set. These query actions are:
a: Identify → compare → summarize
e: Queries scale from one target, to some, to all.

q: 'Which car has the highest horsepower?' is which low-level task?
a: Find extremum
e: Find data cases with an extreme value of an attribute.

q: 'What's the average price of houses in this neighborhood?' is which low-level task?
a: Compute derived value
e: It computes a new number from the data.

q: 'Show only movies released after 2010' is which low-level task?
a: Filter
e: Find data cases that satisfy a condition.

q: 'Is there a relationship between study hours and exam score?' is which low-level task?
a: Correlate
e: Determine useful relationships between attributes.

q: 'Are there groups of similar customers?' is which low-level task?
a: Cluster
e: Find clusters of similar attribute values.

q: 'What's the spread of salaries from lowest to highest?' is which low-level task?
a: Determine range
e: Find the span of values for an attribute.

q: Clicking a county on a map highlights the same county in a linked bar chart. Which interaction is this?
a: Linking (brushing across views)
e: Linked views share selections so you can see one item across multiple representations.

q: Dragging a slider to hide all flights shorter than 500 miles is:
a: Filtering
e: Filtering removes items that don't meet a condition (e.g., Crossfilter).

q: Zooming into a map makes street names and buildings appear that weren't shown before. This is:
a: Semantic zooming
e: Semantic zoom changes what's shown (level of detail); geometric zoom only magnifies.

q: Switching a view from a bar chart to a sorted dot plot is which kind of interaction?
a: Rearranging (changing the encoding)
e: Rearranging changes how the same data is encoded or ordered.

q: Smoothly animating bars to their new positions when the sort order changes helps because:
a: Animated transitions let viewers track items as the view changes
w: It hides changes from the viewer
e: Change over time: transitions preserve context between states.

q: Panning and rotating a view are examples of:
a: Navigation
e: Navigation changes the viewpoint (pan, translate, rotate, zoom).
